(CNN) -- Madagascar's military handed over the reins of the island nation to opposition leader Andry Rajoelina on Wednesday, ending a two-month long political crisis -- but apparently creating a constitutional one. Andry Rajoelina is six years too young to be Madagascar's president under its constitution. Rajoelina, a former disc jockey turned mayor of Madagascar's capital, declared himself president of a transitional government and his supporters pledged to hold elections in two years. But Rajoelina, at 34, is six years too young to be president, according to the country's constitution. Also, the constitution says the head of parliament's upper house must call elections within two months if something happens to the president. Madagascar's former president, Marc Ravalomanana, ceded power to his military Tuesday after insisting over the weekend that he would remain in control. Analysts think Ravalomanana had little choice but to step down once he had lost much of the army's support. The African Union had warned that any power transfer aided by the military would amount to a coup d' etat. The Union has since removed any mention of a coup in its official communique and called on the transitional government to "comply scrupulously with the provisions of the constitution of Madagascar on interim arrangements." Monja Roindefo, the opposition-appointed prime minister, vigorously defended the week's developments on the island, located off the southeastern coast of Africa. "Well, we would like to define what is a coup," he told CNN on Wednesday. "A coup is a group of people or persons who takes the power on behalf of sovereignty, on behalf of the people ... when the representative democracy doesn't work anymore." "As you know, as stated, in the African Union charter, the people have the right to defend itself from an oppression or a dictatorship in Africa," he added. Roindefo said the new government will hold elections but has given itself two years to clean up the process.  Watch more from iReporters and Twitterers on the crisis » . "How could you make an election immediately?" he said. "We need to reform the electoral commission. ... So the 24 months that we have given ourselves is to prepare all these types of elections in order to build a genuine democratic country." The African Union also asked that all steps be taken to ensure the safety of the former president. The opposition leader had called for Ravalomanana's arrest, accusing him of corruption, financial mismanagement and dictatorship. Ravalomanana was first elected in 2001 and won a second term in 2006. To many Malagasy, he represented a new breed of politician -- a self-made millionaire, a no-nonsense business leader. But Ravalomanana maintained his business empire while in office and it was unclear to many where his business interests ended and his political leadership began. His recent purchase of a $60 million airplane further stoked public discontent. Opposition leader Rajoelina was quick to seize on the sentiments and made fiery appeals to the country's impoverished masses. The country was plunged into political instability in January after thousands of people took to the streets to protest rising food prices and what they perceived as autocratic behavior by Ravalomanana. The protests soon degenerated into rioting and looting, and left about 100 people dead.  Watch more on president's resignation » . Soon after, Rajoelina declared that he was in charge of the country. He gave Ravalomanana until early February to step down. The president responded by firing Rajoelina as mayor of the capital, inciting the latter's supporters to once again descend on the streets. More deadly violence followed. Clashes spread to most provincial capitals and other cities across the country, with homes and businesses looted and burned, the U.S. State Department reported. CNN's David McKenzie contributed to this report.

**ANTANANARIVO, Madagascar (CNN)** — Madagascar’s military transferred power to opposition leader Andry Rajoelina on Wednesday, concluding a turbulent two-month political crisis while simultaneously triggering a constitutional dilemma. 

Rajoelina, a 34-year-old former disc jockey and ex-mayor of Madagascar's capital, proclaimed himself president of a transitional government, with his supporters pledging to hold national elections within two years. However, under the nation's constitution, Rajoelina falls six years short of the minimum age requirement for the presidency. Furthermore, constitutional law mandates that should the presidency become vacant, the head of the parliament's upper house must convene elections within two months.

Former President Marc Ravalomanana relinquished power to the military on Tuesday, reversing his weekend vow to remain in office. Political analysts observed that Ravalomanana had little choice but to resign after forfeiting the support of key military factions. 

The African Union (AU) had previously warned that any military-assisted transfer of power would constitute a coup d'état. However, the organization subsequently omitted any mention of a coup in its official communiqué, instead urging the transitional authority to "comply scrupulously with the provisions of the constitution of Madagascar on interim arrangements."

Monja Roindefo, the opposition-appointed prime minister, vigorously defended the week's developments on the Indian Ocean island. 

"Well, we would like to define what is a coup," Roindefo told CNN on Wednesday. "A coup is a group of people or persons who takes the power on behalf of sovereignty, on behalf of the people ... when the representative democracy doesn't work anymore."

He added: "As you know, as stated, in the African Union charter, the people have the right to defend itself from an oppression or a dictatorship in Africa."

Addressing concerns over the election timeline, Roindefo stated that while elections will take place, the interim administration requires two years to reform the system. "How could you make an election immediately?" he argued. "We need to reform the electoral commission. ... So the 24 months that we have given ourselves is to prepare all these types of elections in order to build a genuine democratic country."

Simultaneously, the African Union urged all parties to guarantee the safety of the ousted president. Rajoelina had previously called for Ravalomanana’s arrest, accusing him of corruption, financial mismanagement, and authoritarianism.

First elected in 2001 and re-elected in 2006, Ravalomanana was initially viewed by many Malagasy citizens as a progressive leader—a self-made millionaire and pragmatic corporate executive. However, his decision to maintain his private business empire while in office blurred the lines between his personal commercial interests and governance. Public indignation further intensified following his recent acquisition of a $60 million presidential jet.

Capitalizing on this widespread discontent, Rajoelina delivered impassioned appeals to the nation's impoverished majority. Tensions escalated in January when thousands took to the streets to protest soaring food prices and what they condemned as Ravalomanana's increasingly autocratic rule. The demonstrations rapidly degenerated into violent looting and rioting, resulting in approximately 100 deaths.

Shortly thereafter, Rajoelina declared himself the country's leader, issuing an ultimatum for Ravalomanana to step down by early February. The president retaliated by dismissing Rajoelina from his post as mayor of Antananarivo, inciting opposition supporters to flood the streets once again. 

A new wave of deadly violence followed. According to the U.S. State Department, clashes quickly spread to most provincial capitals and regional centers, where homes and businesses were systematically looted and burned.

*CNN's David McKenzie contributed to this report.*

In March 2009, the island nation of Madagascar plunged into one of the most volatile political chapters in its modern history. Following two months of escalating civil unrest, deadly street protests, and deepening political gridlock, the country’s armed forces intervened, effectively forcing the resignation of President Marc Ravalomanana. In a controversial move, the military leadership bypassed traditional succession protocols and handed executive authority to opposition leader Andry Rajoelina. Designated to lead a two-year transitional government, Rajoelina’s sudden ascension not only reshaped the nation's political landscape but also triggered an immediate constitutional crisis that drew swift and severe international condemnation.

The seeds of the crisis were sown during weeks of fierce confrontation between Ravalomanana’s administration and Rajoelina, the charismatic 34-year-old former mayor of the capital, Antananarivo. Rajoelina had successfully mobilized widespread public discontent, accusing the president of authoritarianism, corruption, and mismanagement of the nation’s economy. As violent clashes between protesters and security forces claimed dozens of lives, the political stalemate threatened to degenerate into full-scale civil conflict. The turning point arrived when key factions within the military mutinied, refusing orders to crack down on anti-government demonstrators and ultimately siding with Rajoelina.

Under immense pressure and surrounded by hostile military forces, President Ravalomanana capitulated on March 17, 2009. In an attempt to maintain a semblance of legal order, he signed a decree transferring presidential powers to a military directorate composed of senior officers. However, the military quickly rejected this mandate. Within hours, the armed forces redirected executive authority to Rajoelina, appointing him president of a newly formed High Transitional Authority (HAT) meant to govern Madagascar for a proposed two-year period leading up to new elections.

This rapid transfer of power immediately collided with Madagascar’s legal framework. Under the Malagasy Constitution of the time, the minimum age required to hold the office of the president was 40. At 34 years old, Rajoelina was six years too young to legally assume the head of state position. Furthermore, the constitution dictated that in the event of a presidential vacancy, power should temporarily pass to the President of the Senate, not a military council or an opposition leader. Although Madagascar’s High Constitutional Court ultimately validated the transition under intense pressure, legal scholars and opposition figures denounced the move as an unconstitutional maneuver and a thinly veiled *coup d'état*.

The international reaction was swift and uncompromising. The African Union (AU) suspended Madagascar’s membership, declaring the event an unconstitutional change of government that violated the bloc's democratic charters. The Southern African Development Community (SADC), the European Union, and the United States echoed these sentiments, refusing to recognize the democratic legitimacy of Rajoelina’s transitional government. Major foreign donors froze international aid—a devastating blow to a country heavily reliant on foreign assistance—demanding a return to constitutional order and inclusive political dialogue.

The events of 2009 set off years of political isolation and economic hardship for Madagascar. What was framed by its perpetrators as a popular liberation and a necessary military intervention to restore order ultimately subverted the rule of law. By prioritizing political expediency over constitutional adherence, the power transfer to Rajoelina severely compromised the nation's democratic institutions and created a diplomatic crisis whose political and economic repercussions would linger for years to come.

**ANTANANARIVO, Madagascar (CNN)** — Madagascar was plunged into deeper political uncertainty on Tuesday after President Marc Ravalomanana officially resigned following months of deadly power struggles, handing control to the military, which swiftly transferred power to young opposition leader Andry Rajoelina.

The dramatic shift in power on the Indian Ocean island nation marks the culmination of weeks of street protests, military mutinies, and international anxiety over what many foreign governments are calling a military-backed coup d'état.

Ravalomanana, who had been holed up in a presidential palace outside the capital of Antananarivo as troops aligned with the opposition surged into the city center, surrendered his authority to a senior military directorate. Within hours, military leaders announced they were endorsing Rajoelina, the 34-year-old former disc jockey and ex-mayor of Antananarivo, as the country’s transitional leader.

Addressing a roaring crowd of tens of thousands of supporters in the capital’s central plaza, Rajoelina proclaimed a new era for the country. "We are free!" he told the cheering masses. "Power belongs to the people."

### Constitutional Crisis Over Age Limit

Despite the celebratory atmosphere among opposition supporters, Rajoelina’s ascension to the presidency immediately triggered intense legal and constitutional debate.

Under Article 46 of the Malagasy Constitution, a candidate running for the office of the presidency must be at least 40 years old. At 34, Rajoelina falls six years short of the constitutional requirement. 

To circumvent the restriction, Rajoelina’s camp suspended key provisions of the constitution and established a "High Transitional Authority," framing his rule not as a standard presidency, but as a temporary stewardship meant to last up to two years before fresh elections are held.

Madagascar’s High Constitutional Court ultimately ratified the power transfer under intense pressure from the military, a move sharply criticized by legal scholars and international observers who argue the maneuver blatantly circumvented the rule of law.

### Opposition Defense and Quotes

Standing alongside Rajoelina throughout the transition was Monja Roindefo, whom the opposition had unilaterally named as Prime Minister during the height of the protests. 

Roindefo strongly rejected allegations that the political transition constituted an unconstitutional military coup, framing the overthrow of Ravalomanana as a necessary act of popular liberation.

"This is not a military coup d'état," Roindefo told reporters in Antananarivo. "This is a direct expression of the democratic will of the people. The population was suffering under an increasingly dictatorial regime that refused to listen. When a government turns its back on its citizens, the people have a right to reclaim their sovereignty."

Roindefo urged the global community not to penalize Madagascar as it attempts to reorganize its government. 

"We call upon our international partners to understand the reality of our situation on the ground," Roindefo added. "We are committed to restoring order, rebuilding our democratic institutions, and holding free, fair elections. Punishing the Malagasy people with sanctions at this critical moment would only deepen their economic hardship."

### Months of Escalating Violence

The crisis began in late January when Rajoelina, nicknamed "TGV" after the French high-speed train for his fast-paced political career, organized massive street protests accusing Ravalomanana of authoritarianism, corruption, and mismanaging the nation's economy. 

Tensions boiled over after the government shut down Rajoelina's private television and radio network, Viva TV. Subsequent clashes between protesters and security forces left more than 100 people dead over two months, including a bloody incident in February when presidential guards opened fire on unarmed demonstrators marching on the presidential palace.

Ravalomanana, a wealthy dairy tycoon who first took power in 2002 after a bitter election dispute, saw his support base crumble as key factions of the military defected to the opposition in recent weeks, refusing orders to crack down on protesters.

### International Backlash

The international community has reacted to the developments with grave concern. 

The African Union (AU) convened an emergency meeting in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, strongly condemning the forced resignation of Ravalomanana and threatening Madagascar with suspension and sanctions over the "unconstitutional change of government."

The Southern African Development Community (SADC) similarly declared that it would not recognize Rajoelina's government, calling the military intervention a dangerous precedent for the region. The United States and the European Union have both indicated that non-humanitarian foreign aid—vital to a country where the vast majority of the population lives on less than $2 a day—could be suspended.

For now, the streets of Antananarivo remain largely calm under the watchful eye of armed soldiers, but the nation faces a long, uncertain road as it grapples with political isolation and the daunting task of rebuilding its fragile democracy.

### BREAKING NEWS: Madagascar Military Hands Power to Opposition Leader Andry Rajoelina Following President's Resignation

**ANTANANARIVO** — In a dramatic climax to months of deadly political turmoil, Madagascar’s military has formally handed executive power to 34-year-old opposition leader Andry Rajoelina, just hours after President Marc Ravalomanana bowed to mounting pressure and resigned.

The move marks a stunning political overthrow on the Indian Ocean island nation, effectively completing a civilian-led, military-backed coup that has sent shockwaves through the region.

The rapid chain of events culminated late yesterday when President Ravalomanana, isolated in his palace and stripped of military support, announced his resignation. In a broadcasted statement, the embattled leader declared he was handing executive authority over to a senior military committee led by Vice Admiral Hyppolite Ramaroson.

However, within hours of receiving the presidential mandate, the military high command rejected the idea of a military junta and instead pledged their full support to Mr. Rajoelina. 

Speaking at a press conference surrounded by army commanders, Vice Admiral Ramaroson announced: "We reject the directorate that Ravalomanana wanted to put in place... We have given full power to Andry Rajoelina to manage the country."

#### Jubilation and Tanks in the Capital

Today, thousands of opposition supporters flooded the streets of the capital, Antananarivo, blowing horns, waving flags, and cheering the young former mayor and DJ, who has spearheaded the opposition movement since January. Armed troops and army vehicles, which stormed the presidential palace on Monday night, remain stationed at key strategic points across the city, though the streets are reported to be calm.

Addressing a roaring crowd of supporters, Rajoelina declared himself the head of a "High Transitional Authority" (HAT) and promised to steer the country toward fresh democratic elections within 24 months.

"Democracy has won," Rajoelina declared to his cheering audience. "We are going to reorganize our nation, rebuild our economy, and bring peace to the Malagasy people."

The whereabouts of the ousted president, Marc Ravalomanana, remain unknown, though local sources suggest he is in hiding at an undisclosed location near the capital, escorted by loyal bodyguards. 

#### Constitutional Questions and International Alarm

Despite the celebrations in Antananarivo, the transfer of power faces significant legal hurdles and international backlash. Under Madagascar’s constitution, the minimum age to hold the presidency is 40; Rajoelina is just 34. However, reports from the capital indicate that the High Constitutional Court has already ratified Rajoelina’s appointment as interim leader, bowing to the military's endorsement.

Foreign diplomats and international bodies have reacted to the power grab with profound concern. 

The African Union (AU) called an emergency meeting in Addis Ababa today to discuss the crisis, with officials threatening to suspend Madagascar from the bloc if the power transfer is deemed an unconstitutional change of government. 

UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon urged all parties to refrain from violence, while the European Union and the United States have warned that foreign aid—which accounts for a massive portion of Madagascar’s national budget—could be suspended if the democratic process is undermined.

#### Months of Bloodshed

The downfall of President Ravalomanana comes after three months of intense political paralysis and violence that has left more than 135 people dead. 

Rajoelina, a charismatic businessman who was elected Mayor of Antananarivo in 2007, launched a crusade against Ravalomanana earlier this year, accusing the billionaire president of autocracy, corruption, and mismanagement of the nation’s resources. The tipping point occurred in February, when presidential guards opened fire on unarmed opposition protesters, killing over 30 people and permanently turning the military against the regime.

While Rajoelina’s supporters view today as a liberation, analysts warn that the island faces an uncertain future. Deprived of foreign aid and facing diplomatic isolation, the new regime in Antananarivo will struggle to stabilize an economy already battered by months of strikes, riots, and the decline of the vital tourism industry.

*This is a developing story. Updates will follow as more details emerge from Antananarivo.*

The military promptly transferred executive authority to Rajoelina, making him Africa’s youngest head of state.

The political crisis, which has crippled the island's vital tourism industry and drawn international outrage, began in late January. What started as protests against rising living costs quickly transformed into a mass movement against Ravalomanana’s government, which opponents accused of corruption, autocratic rule, and mismanaging the country's resources.

Tensions boiled over when the government closed Rajoelina’s private radio and television station, *Viva TV*, after it broadcast an interview with former President Didier Ratsiraka. Rajoelina then launched a campaign of civil disobedience, declaring himself in charge of the country and forming a parallel transitional government.

Public anger was further fueled by controversial government deals, most notably a proposed agreement to lease millions of acres of Madagascan agricultural land to the South Korean conglomerate Daewoo Logistics—a plan Rajoelina heavily criticized and has now pledged to cancel.

The struggle for power took a deadly toll. On February 7, presidential guards fired into a crowd of unarmed opposition protesters marching on the presidential palace, killing more than 30 people. In total, an estimated 135 people have died in political violence over the past two months.

The turning point came earlier this month when a key army unit mutinied, refusing government orders to suppress opposition demonstrators and instead placing their weapons at the disposal of Rajoelina.

### Global Condemnation and Economic Uncertainty

While Rajoelina’s supporters celebrated in the streets of the capital, the international community has responded with swift and stern condemnation.

The African Union (AU) suspended Madagascar’s membership on Friday, declaring the power transfer an "unconstitutional change of government." The Southern African Development Community (SADC) echoed the sentiment, refusing to recognize Rajoelina's leadership.

Madagascar now faces deep political fragmentation and an impending economic crisis. Rajoelina has pledged to hold democratic elections within 24 months, but critics worry his administration lacks legitimacy and legal standing, as the nation’s constitution mandates that the president must be at least 40 years old.

Diplomats warn that without international recognition and foreign aid, the impoverished nation of 20 million people—already reeling from global economic downturns—could slide into deeper instability. 

As the celebrations in Antananarivo wind down, the new regime faces the daunting task of convincing both a divided nation and a skeptical world that it can deliver stability rather than chaos.
